newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Scandal hits rating of Irish government.
newsitem.headline: Scandal hits rating of Irish government.

text.p: The popularity of Ireland's ruling left-right coalition has dropped sharply after a scandal over payments from a top department store chain, according to an opinion poll in the Irish Times on Friday.

The survey showed prime minister John Bruton's Fine Gael party and his junior Labour coalition ally have both taken a dive in popularity ratings in the run-up to a general election expected early next year.

The ratings drop followed the resignation this month of transport minister Michael Lowry after he admitted that Ben Dunne, a former partner in the Dunnes Stores high street chain, paid for the 200,000 Irish pounds ($320,000) renovation of his home.

Fine Gael has also admitted taking cash from Dunne for party funds and a parliamentary committee is to study a list of recipients which is reported by the Irish media to include a senior former government minister of the oppositionn Fianna Fail grouping.
Charles Haughey, prime minister of Ireland for a decade, has denied being the recipient of the mysterious handout, which the Irish media said was paid using a London bank account.
The scandal has raised calls for an investigation into links between party funds and big business and pressure for reform of the way parties get money to fight their election campaigns.
Parliament goes into recess later this month and the names of people who took cash may not be made public until early in 1996, political sources said.
Lowry has yet to explain why Dunne paid for extension work on his private residence but has said he is not guilty of any impropriety.

The Irish Times poll shows that sastisfaction with Bruton's coalition is running at 39 percent, its lowest point in the two years it has been in power, and that 76 percent of people feel the scandal has damaged the government.
Fine Gael's popularity fell by one point to 24 percent, Labour's was trimmed by three points to 10 percent while its Democratic Left coalition ally was unchanged at two percent.

But the opposition parties all showed an improvement in their ratings which will hearten party leaders before an election which could be held after the government unveils what is expected to be a give-away budget in January. An election must be held by November next year.
Fianna Fail, the main opposition party, climbed one point to 46 percent, the small Progressive Democrats gained five points to 11 percent and the Green party was down one at two percent.
